primitives.verbatim_quote: For several reasons including variations in satellite position, environmental factors, and design decisions made by the manufacturer, GPS-enabled watches can produce position measurement errors.
primitives.assumptions: Assumes isotropic Gaussian noise in satellite signal arrival times, uniform atmospheric delay across the route, and constant receiver clock bias.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when geometric dilution of precision (GDOP) exceeds critical threshold, leading to divergence of least-squares position estimate.

primitives.name: GPS Positional Error Bound
primitives.verbatim_quote: Consumer-grade GPS devices are generally only considered to be accurate to approximately 3 meters (10 feet) [5], depending on the number of satellites acquired by the device (more satellites generally result in a more accurate "fix" of position) [2].

primitives.assumptions: Assumes independent, identically distributed rectangular noise; ignores systematic biases from multipath or atmospheric delay.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Error grows linearly with the number of segments in the polyline approximation.

primitives.name: Overestimation Bias Trend
primitives.verbatim_quote: The general trend observed by runners and seen in the literature is that, for most routes, the distance indicated by a GPS watch is slightly greater than the actual distance traveled (Lovett [9] reports 1% overestimation of distance, and therefore pace, as typical).
primitives.assumptions: Assumes positive bias due to random positioning errors inflating chord lengths via the law of cosines.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Bias vanishes as $\Delta t \to 0$; otherwise, it is proportional to $\sigma^2_{GPS}/L$ where $L$ is characteristic length scale.
